title: The Illusion of Control in Modern Markets ft. Yoav Git - Systematic Investor - Ep.393

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/The Illusion of Control in Modern Markets ft. Yoav Git - Systematic Investor - Ep.393.docx

speakers: Yoav Git (co-host, systematic fixed-income researcher; speaker label in captions is Yuval/Yoav)
summary: March 2026 Iran war shock: stocks and bonds sold off together, oil front-end spiked while the back barely moved, CTAs lost little. Git argues CTAs should hedge a common first factor (duration) rather than scale every position when spreads widen, reviews a flow-based excess-volatility paper (value, noise and trend traders), and frames CTA market-universe breadth by correlation and capacity.

completeness_estimate: 0.85 - the first reader captured the crisis, flows, paper and capacity arguments well; missed the EM-algorithm method, the excess-volatility motivation, the initial-positioning dispersion point, the pre-announcement trading remark, the caveat that factor hedging is not worth it for liquid CTAs, and Niels's tracking-error point.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: It ended up being animal welfare and clean drinking water.
claims.claim: Danish election campaign narratives (Greenland, geopolitics expected) ended up dominated by animal welfare and clean water, showing narratives are unpredictable even for narrative-driven markets.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it seems like it's selling off when the war began, but it's almost like it's also selling off now that there might be a de-escalation of the war.
claims.claim: Gold sold off both at war start and on de-escalation news in March 2026, an unpredictable response that supports a rules-based approach.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the spike in oil is at the front of the curve, right?
claims.claim: The oil spike was concentrated at the front of the curve (supply constraints) while Brent three years out barely moved, because the long-run market is over-producing (about 105 mb/d produced vs 102 consumed).

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: We've seen actually a sell-off at the back of the curve, um, which is sort of indicative that what this is happening is a bit of a much more of a risk-off event
claims.claim: Bond sell-offs at long ends of US/UK/EM curves (TY from 114 to 110, more than a year's move in weeks) point to a risk-off event rather than a pure inflation-expectations story.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: oil is traded in a range of say 20-25 dollars a day.
claims.claim: With oil trading a $20-25 daily range (Brent near 120 then 90), execution time of day materially changes P&L and makes tracking one's own model difficult; scenario analysis back to 1998 ranks March 2026 surprise volatility at the top.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: we're going to see correlation between bonds and equity being positive rather than negative
claims.claim: Inflation regimes produce positive stock-bond correlation, so bonds fail as an equity hedge; in March 2026 bonds sold off as much as equities.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: could this be the beginning of another 2022 scenario?
claims.claim: Institutional investors ask whether March 2026 is a 2022 repeat; CTAs only lose less than bonds in surprises and cannot claim protection.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the weakness in the two-year bond auction recently um, in the US government
claims.claim: Weak 2-year US auction and Western fiscal stress suggest inflation is a way to erode debt, making higher yields near-inevitable though timing is unknowable.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the inability to decide for the markets to decide which way it's going um, since 2023.
claims.claim: US rates have been choppy since 2023 (2022 was a clean short), making fixed-income trend trading difficult as moves reverse violently within the month.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: private credit um is under attack. You've seen cracks. You've seen some funds beginning to gate
claims.claim: Private credit funds are gating on redemptions, adding fragility.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's not necessarily just price. It's actually supply.
claims.claim: Energy shocks can be supply availability (rationing) rather than price, affecting activity; Europe and Egypt show vulnerability.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my trend barometer is actually still in a relatively strong level at 52.
claims.claim: Trend barometer 52 (44 markets); BTOP50 -2.25%, SG CTA -2%, SG Trend -2.6%, short-term index about flat; MSCI World -6% in March, bonds -2%, S&P 500 -4.6% in March.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the way he likes to talk about it is weather versus climate.
claims.claim: Back-of-curve oil trading reflects fundamental supply and demand and is insulated from news-cycle shocks (weather vs climate).

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: oil features uh energy features about 6% into the inflation uh directly as a component into into inflation.
claims.claim: Energy has about 6% direct weight in inflation, with secondary effects via food and manufacturing, so the oil curve informs the inflation curve.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: normal CTAs, the the way we would normally manage risk is say, well, the volatility has spiked, and we would sell everything.
claims.claim: In a crisis CTAs scale all positions (longs and shorts) down per market, which is costly when EM spreads widen to about 10 bp; discretionary managers instead close the liquid duration exposure.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: hedging with the TY with the US Treasuries very quickly is actually as effective as you would do then just shrinking your entire portfolios
claims.claim: When correlations spike assets become substitutes, so selling Treasury futures hedges the common first factor as effectively as shrinking the whole book.
claims.direction: short TY futures to hedge directional rates risk

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the difference between which market universe you put
claims.claim: Core-market (highly liquid futures) CTAs can cut duration cheaply in stress; alternative-market CTAs face higher costs, a difference hidden in monthly performance.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: let's say closing closing the book the long short book is like 5% of performance.
claims.claim: Closing a long-short book in the stress cost about 5% of performance in alternative markets, so crisis de-risking is expensive.

correction.issue: Presented as an observed fact. Yoav gave the 5% as an illustrative figure ('let's say') for the cost of closing a long-short alternative-markets book and said he does not have a solution.
correction.fix: Illustratively, closing out a long-short book in alternative markets in stress could cost on the order of 5% of performance, so crisis de-risking there is expensive.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: in times of crisis you have the first factor which has become very which is which is correlated and its volatility is dominate is dominating everything else.
claims.claim: Factor-based risk management: in crises the first (rates) factor dominates volatility, so manage factor risk directly while limiting specific risk per market.
claims.indicator: first principal component of portfolio risk

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: in a liquidity crisis yeah correlations may go to one but you can't get out.
claims.claim: Keeping illiquid positions while hedging with futures is risky because in a liquidity crisis correlations go to one and exits close.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: CTA flows coming in of course volatility as we discussed volatility is gapping we will start taking risk off.
claims.claim: Crisis flow sequence: price gaps on the weekend news, CTAs cut risk as volatility gaps, equities and bonds both sell off.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: suppose I'm a I'm a value trader and I'm I believe in bonds and I'm holding bonds and I'm holding bonds and bond it keeps ticking down
claims.claim: Next in the sequence, value traders holding falling bonds are closed out (long squeeze), then real money buys on stabilisation, then renewed selling after escalation (gilt and Treasury squeezes).

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: CTAs in general pay almost next to no attention to flows
claims.claim: Discretionary traders watch flows closely while CTAs pay almost none, yet CTAs feature in flow models as one of three player types.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the vast majority of volatility is is sort of noise.
claims.claim: Paper conclusion: most volatility is noise; the efficient market hypothesis can hold either because price is right (Shiller) or because there is no true price.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: The player number one is the Shiller player, the fundamental player.
claims.claim: Flow models use three players: value traders (revert to target price), noise traders (inject volatility), and trend followers (trade first derivative, returns).

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: by the way, CTAs or we do not contribute that much to the volatility.
claims.claim: EM-algorithm calibration of the model shows noise is the first order of volatility, value traders second, and trend followers negligible; CTAs create little autocorrelation because footprints are small.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the market is either spent a lot of the time being underpriced or overpriced rather than in the center.
claims.claim: Pendulum picture: trend followers dominate through the centre, value traders dominate at extremes, so markets spend time over- or underpriced.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: half an hour before nonfarm payroll, nobody wants to trade.
claims.claim: Critique: prices gap on news without trading (nonfarm payroll, weekend Iran attack), so explaining all volatility by trading flows ignores genuine jumps in fundamental value.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: Value traders gets get called out just as much as trend followers in terms of risk management.
claims.claim: Critique: assuming a cubic value-trader response (unbounded) is unrealistic because value traders face risk limits too; the paper uses monthly data so cannot inform daily trading.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the amount of risk that we like to put into each market is limited precisely for the same discussion that we had that we don't want to trade against ourselves
claims.claim: Capacity limits risk per market so footprint stays unwindable; larger AUM pushes risk into the biggest markets.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the way CTAs make money is the diversification times the average market shop.
claims.claim: CTA return is diversification times average market Sharpe; if markets are highly correlated, trading only big markets costs little, but if you select low-correlation markets, capacity pushes risk into big markets and cuts effective breadth.
claims.conditions: depends on correlation of the universe

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: you have a 80% correlation and people think, "Oh, that's great.
claims.claim: Replicating the CTA index at 80% correlation is accepted while S&P replication demands 99%, because CTA constituents are opaque.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: it's an iterative process, a little bit like the back propagation process that we have in machine learning these days
claims.claim: The EM (expectation-maximisation) algorithm estimates the parameters of mixed, unlabelled populations by alternating a probabilistic classification of each observation (E step) with re-estimating each distribution (M step) until it converges; it is the calibration tool later used to size the noise, value and trend-trader populations in the flow model.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we know that positioning, initial positioning is so important, and um and you can be lucky, you can be unlucky with how you enter a situation like that
claims.claim: Over the weeks around a shock, dispersion across CTAs is largely driven by initial positioning luck rather than model quality, so short-window results should not be over-read as skill.
claims.indicator: dispersion of CTA returns around shocks
claims.testable: yes - cross-sectional dispersion of manager returns vs prior positioning

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: You should of course do like all the people in oil that apparently traded 10 minutes before the announcement.
claims.claim: Niels notes apparent trading in oil and equities just ahead of policy announcements (S&P selling off, then rallying before a Trump statement), suggesting event-driven reversals can be front-run and are hard for a rules-based process to anticipate; both speakers defer the market-manipulation topic.
claims.conditions: geopolitical and policy headline events, March 2026
claims.testable: partly - event study of pre-announcement returns

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: certainly in the case of like liquid CTA probably not worth the hassle. You would just basically down gear everything
claims.claim: Hedging the common first factor while limiting specific risk per market is a constrained optimisation problem that is probably not worth the effort for a liquid-market CTA, which can simply scale the whole book down.
claims.indicator: factor-based risk reduction vs uniform down-gearing
claims.conditions: liquid core markets where scaling down is cheap
claims.testable: yes - compare crisis de-risking cost and outcome of both methods

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: The problem with this world view is that markets are a lot noisier than what what we would get if everybody would be like that.
claims.claim: If everyone were a Shiller-style value trader prices would jump to the equilibrium and then barely trade, so observed volatility and trading volume far exceed what pure value investing implies (the excess-volatility puzzle), which motivates flow-based models with noise and trend players.
claims.testable: yes - variance-ratio and volatility bound tests

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: when you look at the numbers, that correlation isn't that great. I mean, the tracking error is substantial
claims.claim: Niels argues that although in theory few large markets should replicate a CTA index, in practice replicators' correlation to the index is modest and tracking error substantial.
claims.indicator: tracking error / correlation of replicators to CTA index
claims.conditions: index replication with a small liquid universe
claims.testable: yes - correlation and tracking error of replicator products
